newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPALS - DOWN AFTER FIRM START CRUMBLES.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPALS - DOWN AFTER FIRM START CRUMBLES.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds Tuesday slid an eighth of a point, pushed down from strong gains seen at midday, as fears retail sales data will show consumers were big buyers in July swept through fixed-income markets.

Dollar bonds were up as much as an eighth to a quarter of a point at noon. "Then, when everything went, they gave all that up plus an eighth," said a senior municipal analyst. He added intermediate high grades fell around 0.2.

New issue pricing was mixed, with at least one issuer, Denver Airport, able to raise the size of its offering by $29 million to $371 million because it was seen as offering value in the long-end. The bonds were not repriced by Goldman, Sachs, the underwriter.
But Smith Barney, the underwriter for a $277 million offering by the State of New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority, was forced to raise yields in several maturities.

The $215 million refunding portion of the New York Authority's sale was jettisoned on Monday because the 35- to 40-basis point rise in Treasury bond yields since mid-July meant the agency no longer would have garnered enough savings.

In contrast, Portland, Oregon's surprise refunding of approximately $267 million of sewer bonds was not repriced and in late afternoon trade had only about a $92 million balance. Goldman, Sachs won the issue at a true interest cost of 5.139 percent.

Traders said Denver's sale of airport bonds went more smoothly because it was more attractively priced. But they noted that both the Denver and New York Authority had more difficulty selling bonds in the intermediate sector.

The fixed-income market's strong tone seen earlier in the day was prompted by a few signs of slowing wage inflation pressures and the possibility manufacturing was slipping in the Southeast, though the latter report was attributed to seasonal factors.
The second quarter 2.4 percent unit labor cost increase was below forecasts of 2.7 percent.
The Richmond Federal Reserve shipments index for July fell to minus 10 from plus 15 in June. The new orders index was seven, down from June's reading of 11.

The supply of new municipal bonds was expected to drop fairly sharply on Wednesday, as most issuers tried to get their sales completed before a string of economic data, which will be closely examined for any signs inflation is rising.

Redbook's retail sales index late Tuesday showed U.S. adjusted retail sales up 0.9 percent in the August 9 week. This worried traders who were waiting for the latest retail sales data, due out 0830 EDT on Wednesday, because they said some economists have raised their projections.

A Reuter poll of economists showed they look for consumer spending to climb 0.7 percent, with a 0.5 percent rise seen when autos are excluded. Both forecasts were higher than June's report, which showed retail sales gained 0.5 percent overall, with the ex-autos measure firming 0.3 percent.

One of the more important inflation gauges, producer prices for July, also was slated for 0830 EDT on Wednesday. They were forecast at up 0.1 percent, an increase from June's slip of minus 0.1 percent.
And on Thursday at 0830 EDT, consumer prices were scheduled. They were projected at up 0.2 percent, a slightly bigger rise than June's 0.1 percent increase.
In the secondary market, Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority bonds of 2024, which pay a five percent coupon, were bid at 5.56 percent, NET, up one basis point.
And Muncipal Electricity Authority Georgia bonds of 2026, with a five percent coupon, were offered at 5.45 percent, NET. On Monday, the bonds were bid at 5.54 percent, NET.
In Chicago futures markets, September municipal bond futures closed off five ticks at 118-25/32, while September Treasury bond futures closed down nine ticks at 112-15/32.
This left the MOB spread at plus 202 ticks, up four ticks from late Monday.
